summary: This is an answer key for Assignment #2 of a Fall 2016 Microeconomic Theory I course (ECON 501). It works through problems on the weak axiom of revealed preference (WARP) for random, average, and conspicuous demand functions; a Cobb-Douglas consumer's utility maximization, expenditure minimization and duality; a discrete and continuous choice between two types of labor; and a Stone-Geary utility exercise from Nicholson and Snyder. The solutions use Lagrangians, first-order conditions and budget-share limits to reach their conclusions.
one_line: Answer key for a fall 2016 graduate microeconomics homework covering WARP, Cobb-Douglas duality, labor-choice models and Stone-Geary utility.
key_facts: Random demand violates WARP, because the old consumption bundle can remain affordable under the new prices and wealth.
Average demand satisfies WARP, proven by contradiction using the midpoint of the budget line, where x1 = w/(2p1).
Conspicuous demand violates WARP, as shown by the figure covering both cases of the demand function.
For the Cobb-Douglas utility u(x1,x2)=x1^alpha x2^(1-alpha), the Walrasian demand for good 1 is x1(p,w)=alpha*w/p1.
The indirect utility function for the Cobb-Douglas consumer is v(p1,p2,w) = (alpha/p1)^alpha((1-alpha)/p2)^(1-alpha) w.
The expenditure function for the Cobb-Douglas consumer is e(p1,p2,u) = (1/alpha)^alpha (1/(1-alpha))^(1-alpha) p1^alpha p2^(1-alpha) u.
The answer key shows that Walrasian and Hicksian demands coincide when wealth equals the minimum expenditure, and that v(p1,p2,e(p1,p2,u)) = u.
In the discrete labor choice, the individual with one unit of time chooses among no work, L1 = 1/3 (wage w1), or L2 = 1/3 (wage w2 > w1).
In the continuous labor choice, the first-order conditions are (w1/p)uc - ul + uL1 = 0 and (w2/p)uc - ul + uL2 = 0.
Positive supply of both labor types requires (w1-w2)/p * uc = uL2 - uL1, so with w2 > w1 it needs uL1 > uL2.
The labor model combines effort and boredom into the single term uLi and cannot separate their effects without distinguishing them in the utility function.
Problem 2 is Exercise 4.12 from Nicholson and Snyder, a Stone-Geary utility problem where utility is negative for x < x0.
In the Stone-Geary answer key, budget shares approach alpha and beta as income approaches infinity: lim p_x x / I = alpha and lim p_y y / I = beta.
The handout is labeled Microeconomic Theory I, Assignment #2 - Answer Key.
